In August 2004, Adam Curry launched his show _Daily Source Code_, focused on chronicling his everyday life, delivering news, and discussions about the development of podcasting. Curry promoted new and emerging internet audio shows in an attempt to gain traction in the development of what would come to be known as podcasting.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Podcast#cite_note-24)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Podcast#cite_note-25)_Daily Source Code_ was initially directed at podcast developers. As its audience became interested in the format, these developers were inspired to create and produce their own projects and a community of pioneer podcasters quickly developed.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Podcast#cite_note-Origins-26)
iPodderX, released in September 2004 by August Trometer and based on earlier work by Ray Slakinski, was the first GUI application for podcasts.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Podcast#cite_note-wired1-27)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Podcast#cite_note-28)
In June 2005, [Apple](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc. "Apple Inc.") released iTunes 4.9, which added formal support for podcasts, thus negating the need to use a separate program in order to download and transfer them to a mobile device. Additionally, Apple issued cease-and-desist orders to many podcast application developers and service providers for using the term "iPod" or "Pod" in their products' names.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Podcast#cite_note-29)

In February 2006, following London radio station LBC's successful launch of the first premium-podcasting platform, LBC Plus, there was widespread acceptance that podcasting had considerable commercial potential. UK comedian Ricky Gervais, whose first season of _The Ricky Gervais Show_ became a big hit, launched a new series of the popular podcast. The first series of _The Ricky Gervais Show_ podcast had been freely distributed by the Positive Internet Company and marketed through _The Guardian_ newspaper's website, and it was the world's most successful podcast for several years, eventually gaining more than 300 million unique downloads by March 2011.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Podcast#cite_note-30) The second series of the podcast was distributed through audible.co.uk and was the first major podcast to charge consumers to download the show (at a rate of 95 pence per half-hour episode). Even in its new subscription format, _The Ricky Gervais Show_ was regularly the most-downloaded podcast on iTunes. _The Adam Carolla Show_ claimed a new Guinness world record, with total downloads approaching 60 million, but Guinness failed to acknowledge that Gervais's podcast had more than 5 times as many downloads as Carolla's show at the time that this new record was supposedly set.
The logo used by [Apple](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc. "Apple Inc.") to represent podcasting in Apple Podcasts
By 2007, audio podcasts were doing what was historically accomplished via radio broadcasts, which had been the source of radio talk shows and news programs since the 1930s. This shift occurred as a result of the evolution of internet capabilities along with increased consumer access to cheaper hardware and software for audio recording and editing.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Podcast#cite_note-Digital-31)

As of early 2019, the podcasting industry still generated little overall revenue,[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Podcast#cite_note-Smith2019-32) although the number of persons listening to podcasts continued to grow steadily. Edison Research, which issues the Podcast Consumer quarterly tracking-report, estimated that 90 million persons in the U.S. had listened to a podcast in January 2019.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Podcast#cite_note-EdisonResearch2019-33) In 2020, 58% of the population of South Korea and 40% of the population of Spain had listened to a podcast in the last month; 12.5% of the UK population had listened to a podcast in the last week; and 22% of the United States population listened to at least one podcast weekly.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Podcast#cite_note-34) During the 2020s, podcasting grew substantially as a commercial industry, with increasing advertising revenue and the growing popularity of video podcasts.

### IP issues in trademark and patent law
[edit]

### IP issues in trademark and patent law
#### Trademark applications
[edit]
Between February 10 and March 25, 2005, Shae Spencer Management, LLC of Fairport, New York filed a trademark application to register the term "podcast" for an "online pre-recorded radio program over the internet". On September 9, 2005, the United States Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO) rejected the application, citing Wikipedia's entry on "Podcast" as describing the history of the term. The company amended their application in March 2006, but the USPTO rejected the amended application as not sufficiently differentiated from the original. In November 2006, the application was marked as abandoned.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Podcast#cite_note-35)

### IP issues in trademark and patent law
#### Apple trademark protections
[edit]
On September 26, 2004, it was reported that [Apple Inc.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc. "Apple Inc.") had started to crack down on businesses using the string "POD", in product and company names. Apple sent a cease-and-desist letter that week to Podcast Ready, Inc., which markets an application known as "myPodder".[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Podcast#cite_note-36) Lawyers for Apple contended that the term "pod" had been used by the public to refer to Apple's music player so extensively that it falls under Apple's trademark cover.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Podcast#cite_note-37) Such activity was speculated to be part of a bigger campaign for Apple to expand the scope of its existing iPod trademark, which included trademarking "IPOD", "IPODCAST", and "POD".[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Podcast#cite_note-38) On November 16, 2006, the Apple Trademark Department stated that "Apple does not object to third-party usage of the generic term 'podcast' to accurately refer to podcasting services" and that "Apple does not license the term". However, no statement was made as to whether or not Apple believed they held rights to it.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Podcast#cite_note-39)

### IP issues in trademark and patent law
#### Personal Audio lawsuits
[edit]
Personal Audio, a company referred to as a "patent troll" by the Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF),[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Podcast#cite_note-EFF-40) filed a patent on podcasting in 2009 for a claimed invention in 1996.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Podcast#cite_note-41) In February 2013, Personal Audio started suing high-profile podcasters for royalties,[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Podcast#cite_note-EFF-40) including _The Adam Carolla Show_ and the _HowStuffWorks_ podcasts.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Podcast#cite_note-42) In October 2013, the EFF filed a petition with the US Trademark Office to invalidate the Personal Audio patent.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Podcast#cite_note-43) On August 18, 2014, the EFF announced that Adam Carolla had settled with Personal Audio.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Podcast#cite_note-44) Finally, on April 10, 2015, the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office invalidated five provisions of Personal Audio's podcasting patent.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Podcast#cite_note-45)

_**The Last Podcast on the Left**_ is a weekly podcast on the Last Podcast Network[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Last_Podcast_on_the_Left#cite_note-1) featuring podcast producer and researcher Marcus Parks, comedian and actor Henry Zebrowski, and comedian Ed Larson, three longtime friends. Episodes have explored the topics of serial killers, cults, conspiracy theories, UFO sightings, ghosts, cryptids, the occult, and readings of fan-submitted creepypastas.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Last_Podcast_on_the_Left#cite_note-2) The name is a reference to the 1972 horror movie _The Last House on the Left_.
Episodes explore real and imagined horror, with a typical runtime of one to two hours. The show releases two episodes weekly: a main episode and a side story episode.
Main episodes, currently hosted by Marcus Parks, Henry Zebrowski, and Ed Larson and formerly hosted by Ben Kissel, are focused on a singular topic and multiple episodes may be dedicated to one topic. Side Stories are typically hosted by Larson and Zebrowski (previously only Kissel and Zebrowski) and cover weekly true crime and other unusual news stories, with an additional “Hero of the Week” segment and often a “Listener Emails” segment. Occasionally, guests are invited onto the show for interviews, including Dan Aykroyd.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Last_Podcast_on_the_Left#cite_note-3)

The opening theme of the podcast features a snippet from serial killer Jeffrey Dahmer who utters the line, "That's when the cannibalism started." It also includes the line and subsequent advertisement transition "Rise from your grave!" uttered by Zeus from the Sega action game _Altered Beast_ (1988). The closing theme is Al Bowlly's "Midnight, the Stars and You", a reference to _The Shining_ (1980).
Several repeat characters are present on the podcast (primarily voiced by Zebrowski) such as "Detective Popcorn" (the semi-erotic food-focused and incompetent police detective); Charles Ng (a notorious serial killer); "Terry the Gnome", "The Bone-Slicer"; and Minnie and Nannie Williams (victims of serial killer H. H. Holmes).[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Last_Podcast_on_the_Left#cite_note-heavy-4)

**Ed Larson** (born October 9, 1981)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Last_Podcast_on_the_Left#cite_note-11) is an American comedian, writer and actor. Larson was made a temporary co-host of _The Last Podcast on the Left_ in late 2023, following Ben Kissel's departure, and eventually became a permanent co-host of the show. He was previously a member of Zebrowski's sketch comedy troupe Murderfist.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Last_Podcast_on_the_Left#cite_note-12)
Larson also co-hosts another Last Podcast Network show called _The Brighter Side_ with Amber Nelson, a show exploring and talking about the brighter side of a topic they choose every week.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Last_Podcast_on_the_Left#cite_note-13)

Outside of the Last Podcast Network, he performs stand-up comedy,[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Last_Podcast_on_the_Left#cite_note-14) and has released a documentary called "How America Killed My Mother". The documentary explores how the health insurance and banking systems in the United States contributed to his mother's death.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Last_Podcast_on_the_Left#cite_note-15)

**Ben Kissel** is an American comedian and former politician. Kissel was born in Fargo, North Dakota and raised in Stevens Point, Wisconsin and attended the University of Wisconsin-Milwaukee, where he received a degree in political science.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Last_Podcast_on_the_Left#cite_note-16)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Last_Podcast_on_the_Left#cite_note-17)
After co-creating _The Last Podcast on the Left_ in 2011, Kissel would continue to co-host the show until 2023.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Last_Podcast_on_the_Left#cite_note-:0-18) In 2017, Kissel ran for Brooklyn borough president as the candidate for the Reform Party but lost with 1.79% (6,017) of the vote.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Last_Podcast_on_the_Left#cite_note-19) Kissel also co-hosted _Abe Lincoln's Top Hat_, a political podcast that ran under the Last Podcast Network.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Last_Podcast_on_the_Left#cite_note-20)
On October 4, 2023, it was announced that Kissel would no longer be part of the podcast or the Last Podcast Network. This came following allegations of abuse.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Last_Podcast_on_the_Left#cite_note-:3-21)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Last_Podcast_on_the_Left#cite_note-:1-22)_(See Co-host abuse allegations)_

### Ben Kissel (formerly)
_Last Podcast on the Left_ was launched in 2011[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Last_Podcast_on_the_Left#cite_note-heavy-4) as a conversation between friends who love horror movies. The name was inspired by the horror movie _The Last House on the Left_. The podcast's discussions have delved into topics including aliens, cryptids and other macabre topics.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Last_Podcast_on_the_Left#cite_note-:0-18)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Last_Podcast_on_the_Left#cite_note-23)
In 2017, _The Last Podcast on the Left_ received the People's Voice Webby in the Podcasts & Digital Audio (Comedy) category.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Last_Podcast_on_the_Left#cite_note-24)
In 2018, they filmed their first live show at Thalia Hall in Chicago, IL. In 2019, they filmed their second live show in New Orleans, LA.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Last_Podcast_on_the_Left#cite_note-25) The hosts have toured extensively in the US and internationally, including Iceland,[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Last_Podcast_on_the_Left#cite_note-26) Australia,[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Last_Podcast_on_the_Left#cite_note-27) and Canada[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Last_Podcast_on_the_Left#cite_note-28) for live events.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Last_Podcast_on_the_Left#cite_note-:2-10)
On November 19, 2019, it was announced that the show was moving exclusively to Spotify[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Last_Podcast_on_the_Left#cite_note-29) for ad-sponsored episodes. This arrangement was short-lived, ending in October 2021.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Last_Podcast_on_the_Left#cite_note-:0-18)

### Ben Kissel (formerly)
In 2020, Houghton Mifflin Harcourt released _The Last Book on the Left_,[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Last_Podcast_on_the_Left#cite_note-30)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Last_Podcast_on_the_Left#cite_note-31) written by Kissel, Parks, and Zebrowski, and illustrated by Tom Neely.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Last_Podcast_on_the_Left#cite_note-32)[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Last_Podcast_on_the_Left#cite_note-33) The book debuted at number three on the _New York Times_ Bestseller List under Hardcover nonfiction.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Last_Podcast_on_the_Left#cite_note-34)
On September 13, 2023, it was announced that co-host Ben Kissel would be "going into treatment" for his mental and physical health, and would not feature on the podcast until his treatment was completed. This came following accusations of abuse by a former girlfriend, though this was not explicitly stated as a contributing factor for his leave.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Last_Podcast_on_the_Left#cite_note-35)[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Last_Podcast_on_the_Left#cite_note-36) On October 4, 2023, it was announced that Kissel would no longer be part of the podcast or the Last Podcast Network.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Last_Podcast_on_the_Left#cite_note-:3-21)

### Co-host abuse allegations
[edit]
On October 12, 2023, _Rolling Stone_ released an article that outlined allegations against former _Last Podcast on the Left_ co-host Ben Kissel, which included multiple alleged instances of sexual misconduct and verbal and physical abuse against women over the span of several years. The article further included testimony of former and current associates of Kissel who allege that he had issues with alcoholism, some of whom claimed that it would lead to drastic changes in his personality. Other individuals contacted by _Rolling Stone_ went against many of the allegations, such as denying Kissel's personality would drastically change by consuming alcohol or attesting that they had never seen Kissel be abusive towards a woman or violent in any capacity.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Last_Podcast_on_the_Left#cite_note-:1-22)
Former acquaintances also implied that there may have been a "willful blindness" towards Kissel's alleged behaviour and alcohol abuse among The Last Podcast Network, though this was disputed by individuals close to the network. One person outlined in the article claimed that Kissel's substance abuse was a known issue in the workplace, and lengthy discussions over it had taken place over a "seven year period." They further stated that this had become enough of an issue that discussions were being made to remove Kissel from the show weeks before his eventual departure. Parks and Zebrowski are specifically named as individuals who attempted to discuss and intervene in Kissel's drinking problems.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Last_Podcast_on_the_Left#cite_note-:1-22) A statement was released on the _Last Podcast on the Left_Instagram page on October 14, in which it was claimed that they had no knowledge of the alleged abusive behavior.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Last_Podcast_on_the_Left#cite_note-37)
In the same article, a statement written by Kissel was published, where he denied all allegations of abuse, but conceded he had been using alcohol to "cope with childhood trauma," and was in rehab to deal with his issues.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Last_Podcast_on_the_Left#cite_note-:1-22)

_**The Last Podcast on the Left**_ is a weekly podcast on the Last Podcast Network[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Last_Podcast_on_the_Left#cite_note-1) featuring podcast producer and researcher Marcus Parks, comedian and actor Henry Zebrowski, and comedian Ed Larson, three longtime friends. Episodes have explored the topics of serial killers, cults, conspiracy theories, UFO sightings, ghosts, cryptids, the occult, and readings of fan-submitted creepypastas.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Last_Podcast_on_the_Left#cite_note-2) The name is a reference to the 1972 horror movie _The Last House on the Left_.
Episodes explore real and imagined horror, with a typical runtime of one to two hours. The show releases two episodes weekly: a main episode and a side story episode.
Main episodes, currently hosted by Marcus Parks, Henry Zebrowski, and Ed Larson and formerly hosted by Ben Kissel, are focused on a singular topic and multiple episodes may be dedicated to one topic. Side Stories are typically hosted by Larson and Zebrowski (previously only Kissel and Zebrowski) and cover weekly true crime and other unusual news stories, with an additional “Hero of the Week” segment and often a “Listener Emails” segment. Occasionally, guests are invited onto the show for interviews, including Dan Aykroyd.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Last_Podcast_on_the_Left#cite_note-3)

**Ben Kissel** is an American comedian and former politician. Kissel was born in Fargo, North Dakota and raised in Stevens Point, Wisconsin and attended the University of Wisconsin-Milwaukee, where he received a degree in political science.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Last_Podcast_on_the_Left#cite_note-16)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Last_Podcast_on_the_Left#cite_note-17)
After co-creating _The Last Podcast on the Left_ in 2011, Kissel would continue to co-host the show until 2023.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Last_Podcast_on_the_Left#cite_note-:0-18) In 2017, Kissel ran for Brooklyn borough president as the candidate for the Reform Party but lost with 1.79% (6,017) of the vote.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Last_Podcast_on_the_Left#cite_note-19) Kissel also co-hosted _Abe Lincoln's Top Hat_, a political podcast that ran under the Last Podcast Network.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Last_Podcast_on_the_Left#cite_note-20)

### Ben Kissel (formerly)
_Last Podcast on the Left_ was launched in 2011[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Last_Podcast_on_the_Left#cite_note-heavy-4) as a conversation between friends who love horror movies. The name was inspired by the horror movie _The Last House on the Left_. The podcast's discussions have delved into topics including aliens, cryptids and other macabre topics.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Last_Podcast_on_the_Left#cite_note-:0-18)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Last_Podcast_on_the_Left#cite_note-23)
In 2017, _The Last Podcast on the Left_ received the People's Voice Webby in the Podcasts & Digital Audio (Comedy) category.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Last_Podcast_on_the_Left#cite_note-24)
In 2018, they filmed their first live show at Thalia Hall in Chicago, IL. In 2019, they filmed their second live show in New Orleans, LA.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Last_Podcast_on_the_Left#cite_note-25) The hosts have toured extensively in the US and internationally, including Iceland,[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Last_Podcast_on_the_Left#cite_note-26) Australia,[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Last_Podcast_on_the_Left#cite_note-27) and Canada[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Last_Podcast_on_the_Left#cite_note-28) for live events.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Last_Podcast_on_the_Left#cite_note-:2-10)
On November 19, 2019, it was announced that the show was moving exclusively to Spotify[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Last_Podcast_on_the_Left#cite_note-29) for ad-sponsored episodes. This arrangement was short-lived, ending in October 2021.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Last_Podcast_on_the_Left#cite_note-:0-18)

### Co-host abuse allegations
[edit]
On October 12, 2023, _Rolling Stone_ released an article that outlined allegations against former _Last Podcast on the Left_ co-host Ben Kissel, which included multiple alleged instances of sexual misconduct and verbal and physical abuse against women over the span of several years. The article further included testimony of former and current associates of Kissel who allege that he had issues with alcoholism, some of whom claimed that it would lead to drastic changes in his personality. Other individuals contacted by _Rolling Stone_ went against many of the allegations, such as denying Kissel's personality would drastically change by consuming alcohol or attesting that they had never seen Kissel be abusive towards a woman or violent in any capacity.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Last_Podcast_on_the_Left#cite_note-:1-22)
Former acquaintances also implied that there may have been a "willful blindness" towards Kissel's alleged behaviour and alcohol abuse among The Last Podcast Network, though this was disputed by individuals close to the network. One person outlined in the article claimed that Kissel's substance abuse was a known issue in the workplace, and lengthy discussions over it had taken place over a "seven year period." They further stated that this had become enough of an issue that discussions were being made to remove Kissel from the show weeks before his eventual departure. Parks and Zebrowski are specifically named as individuals who attempted to discuss and intervene in Kissel's drinking problems.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Last_Podcast_on_the_Left#cite_note-:1-22) A statement was released on the _Last Podcast on the Left_Instagram page on October 14, in which it was claimed that they had no knowledge of the alleged abusive behavior.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Last_Podcast_on_the_Left#cite_note-37)
In the same article, a statement written by Kissel was published, where he denied all allegations of abuse, but conceded he had been using alcohol to "cope with childhood trauma," and was in rehab to deal with his issues.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Last_Podcast_on_the_Left#cite_note-:1-22)

In August 2004, Adam Curry launched his show _Daily Source Code_, focused on chronicling his everyday life, delivering news, and discussions about the development of podcasting. Curry promoted new and emerging internet audio shows in an attempt to gain traction in the development of what would come to be known as podcasting.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Podcast#cite_note-24)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Podcast#cite_note-25)_Daily Source Code_ was initially directed at podcast developers. As its audience became interested in the format, these developers were inspired to create and produce their own projects and a community of pioneer podcasters quickly developed.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Podcast#cite_note-Origins-26)
iPodderX, released in September 2004 by August Trometer and based on earlier work by Ray Slakinski, was the first GUI application for podcasts.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Podcast#cite_note-wired1-27)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Podcast#cite_note-28)
In June 2005, [Apple](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc. "Apple Inc.") released iTunes 4.9, which added formal support for podcasts, thus negating the need to use a separate program in order to download and transfer them to a mobile device. Additionally, Apple issued cease-and-desist orders to many podcast application developers and service providers for using the term "iPod" or "Pod" in their products' names.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Podcast#cite_note-29)
texts.5:
In February 2006, following London radio station LBC's successful launch of the first premium-podcasting platform, LBC Plus, there was widespread acceptance that podcasting had considerable commercial potential. UK comedian Ricky Gervais, whose first season of _The Ricky Gervais Show_ became a big hit, launched a new series of the popular podcast. The first series of _The Ricky Gervais Show_ podcast had been freely distributed by the Positive Internet Company and marketed through _The Guardian_ newspaper's website, and it was the world's most successful podcast for several years, eventually gaining more than 300 million unique downloads by March 2011.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Podcast#cite_note-30) The second series of the podcast was distributed through audible.co.uk and was the first major podcast to charge consumers to download the show (at a rate of 95 pence per half-hour episode). Even in its new subscription format, _The Ricky Gervais Show_ was regularly the most-downloaded podcast on iTunes. _The Adam Carolla Show_ claimed a new Guinness world record, with total downloads approaching 60 million, but Guinness failed to acknowledge that Gervais's podcast had more than 5 times as many downloads as Carolla's show at the time that this new record was supposedly set.
The logo used by [Apple](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc. "Apple Inc.") to represent podcasting in Apple Podcasts
By 2007, audio podcasts were doing what was historically accomplished via radio broadcasts, which had been the source of radio talk shows and news programs since the 1930s. This shift occurred as a result of the evolution of internet capabilities along with increased consumer access to cheaper hardware and software for audio recording and editing.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Podcast#cite_note-Digital-31)
texts.6: As of early 2019, the podcasting industry still generated little overall revenue,[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Podcast#cite_note-Smith2019-32) although the number of persons listening to podcasts continued to grow steadily. Edison Research, which issues the Podcast Consumer quarterly tracking-report, estimated that 90 million persons in the U.S. had listened to a podcast in January 2019.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Podcast#cite_note-EdisonResearch2019-33) In 2020, 58% of the population of South Korea and 40% of the population of Spain had listened to a podcast in the last month; 12.5% of the UK population had listened to a podcast in the last week; and 22% of the United States population listened to at least one podcast weekly.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Podcast#cite_note-34) During the 2020s, podcasting grew substantially as a commercial industry, with increasing advertising revenue and the growing popularity of video podcasts.

### IP issues in trademark and patent law
#### Trademark applications
[edit]
Between February 10 and March 25, 2005, Shae Spencer Management, LLC of Fairport, New York filed a trademark application to register the term "podcast" for an "online pre-recorded radio program over the internet". On September 9, 2005, the United States Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO) rejected the application, citing Wikipedia's entry on "Podcast" as describing the history of the term. The company amended their application in March 2006, but the USPTO rejected the amended application as not sufficiently differentiated from the original. In November 2006, the application was marked as abandoned.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Podcast#cite_note-35)
texts.9:
### IP issues in trademark and patent law
#### Apple trademark protections
[edit]
On September 26, 2004, it was reported that [Apple Inc.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc. "Apple Inc.") had started to crack down on businesses using the string "POD", in product and company names. Apple sent a cease-and-desist letter that week to Podcast Ready, Inc., which markets an application known as "myPodder".[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Podcast#cite_note-36) Lawyers for Apple contended that the term "pod" had been used by the public to refer to Apple's music player so extensively that it falls under Apple's trademark cover.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Podcast#cite_note-37) Such activity was speculated to be part of a bigger campaign for Apple to expand the scope of its existing iPod trademark, which included trademarking "IPOD", "IPODCAST", and "POD".[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Podcast#cite_note-38) On November 16, 2006, the Apple Trademark Department stated that "Apple does not object to third-party usage of the generic term 'podcast' to accurately refer to podcasting services" and that "Apple does not license the term". However, no statement was made as to whether or not Apple believed they held rights to it.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Podcast#cite_note-39)
texts.10:
### IP issues in trademark and patent law
#### Personal Audio lawsuits
[edit]
Personal Audio, a company referred to as a "patent troll" by the Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF),[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Podcast#cite_note-EFF-40) filed a patent on podcasting in 2009 for a claimed invention in 1996.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Podcast#cite_note-41) In February 2013, Personal Audio started suing high-profile podcasters for royalties,[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Podcast#cite_note-EFF-40) including _The Adam Carolla Show_ and the _HowStuffWorks_ podcasts.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Podcast#cite_note-42) In October 2013, the EFF filed a petition with the US Trademark Office to invalidate the Personal Audio patent.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Podcast#cite_note-43) On August 18, 2014, the EFF announced that Adam Carolla had settled with Personal Audio.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Podcast#cite_note-44) Finally, on April 10, 2015, the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office invalidated five provisions of Personal Audio's podcasting patent.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Podcast#cite_note-45)

Dec 3 · Subscriber Early Access ### Jataka Tales : Stories of the Buddha's Many Births The Jataka Tales are an ancient collection of stories, narrating the past lives of the Buddha Siddharta Gautama. The stories exist in different forms across the Buddhist world. In this edition, Misha Glenny and his guests explore the Pali collection of around 550 Jataka Tales. On the night of his Enlightenment, before he became the Buddha, Siddharta Gautama is believed to have gained the ability to recall each of his past lives. In the Jataka collection, he uses the stories of these past lives to relay his teachings. Each rebirth saw him take a different form, he could be an animal like a monkey or a fish, he could be a Prince or even a God. The battle took place on 17th September 1862, less than 100 miles from Washington D.C. The conflict had been going on for over a year, and there had been a string of successes by the rebel Confederate Army against Union forces. The Confederates were a group of Southern States that had seceded from the United States of America over their right to continue the institution of slavery. 3d ago ### Megalosaurus The first dinosaur to ever be scientifically named, almost 20 years before we even had the word ‘dinosaur’. In 1824, the geologist and priest William Buckland (1784-1856) stood before the Geological Society of London and announced something that would kickstart two centuries of dinosaur science. He’d been studying large, fossilised bones which didn’t resemble those of any living animal - and, as he told his rapt audience at that meeting, he had a new name for this mysterious and unusual creature: Megalosaurus. Misha Glenny and his guests discuss why the 19th century was such profound period of theological and scientific change, and how our understanding of mid Jurassic dinosaurs has changed since. This In Our Time episode examines the story of a dinosaur that led to palaeontology as we know it today. The discussion explores the influential roles of William and Mary Buckland, how we learn about animals from over 160 million years ago, and why you’d never have seen a Megalosaurus and a Tyrannosaurus Rex together. 8.   Oct 26 ### Archive: Dark Matter, the mysterious substance in space Dark Matter is a proposed form of matter that does not absorb, reflect or emit light. It is known to make up 27% of our universe, while the matter that makes up stars and galaxies accounts for only 5%. In this archive episode, first released in March 2015, Melvyn Bragg and his guests discuss dark matter, the mysterious and invisible substance existing throughout the Universe. In 1932 the Dutch astronomer Jan Oort noticed that the speed at which galaxies moved was at odds with the amount of material they appeared to contain. He hypothesized that much of this 'missing' matter was simply invisible to telescopes. Today astronomers and particle physicists are still fascinated by the search for dark matter and the question of what it is. One leading theory is that Dark Matter is made up of WIMPS (Weakly Interacting Massive Particles) that are big, heavy and move slowly, interacting with gravity but not other particles. Scientists have developed multiple theories about the make up of this substance, and they are able to test them through remarkable computer modelling that simulates the construction of the universe. Dec 3 · Subscriber Early Access ### Jataka Tales : Stories of the Buddha's Many Births The Jataka Tales are an ancient collection of stories, narrating the past lives of the Buddha Siddharta Gautama. The stories exist in different forms across the Buddhist world. In this edition, Misha Glenny and his guests explore the Pali collection of around 550 Jataka Tales. On the night of his Enlightenment, before he became the Buddha, Siddharta Gautama is believed to have gained the ability to recall each of his past lives. In the Jataka collection, he uses the stories of these past lives to relay his teachings. Each rebirth saw him take a different form, he could be an animal like a monkey or a fish, he could be a Prince or even a God. Jatakas have existed for thousands of years, and they are a cornerstone of Buddhist literature, art and religious teachings. The stories contain a multitude of recurring characters in the community around the Buddha, and their influence exists beyond Buddhism into other cultures around the world. The battle took place on 17th September 1862, less than 100 miles from Washington D.C. The conflict had been going on for over a year, and there had been a string of successes by the rebel Confederate Army against Union forces. The Confederates were a group of Southern States that had seceded from the United States of America over their right to continue the institution of slavery. This secession was rejected by US President Abraham Lincoln, who was committed to maintaining the Union. Despite heavy Union casualties, Antietam has been called the ‘crossroads of freedom’ by historians. It played a crucial role in the release of the Emancipation Proclamation against slavery, which was described by Lincoln as ‘the great event of the 19th Century’. In 1824, the geologist and priest William Buckland (1784-1856) stood before the Geological Society of London and announced something that would kickstart two centuries of dinosaur science. He’d been studying large, fossilised bones which didn’t resemble those of any living animal - and, as he told his rapt audience at that meeting, he had a new name for this mysterious and unusual creature: Megalosaurus. Misha Glenny and his guests discuss why the 19th century was such profound period of theological and scientific change, and how our understanding of mid Jurassic dinosaurs has changed since. This In Our Time episode examines the story of a dinosaur that led to palaeontology as we know it today. The discussion explores the influential roles of William and Mary Buckland, how we learn about animals from over 160 million years ago, and why you’d never have seen a Megalosaurus and a Tyrannosaurus Rex together. 8.   Oct 26 ### Archive: Dark Matter, the mysterious substance in space Dark Matter is a proposed form of matter that does not absorb, reflect or emit light. It is known to make up 27% of our universe, while the matter that makes up stars and galaxies accounts for only 5%. In this archive episode, first released in March 2015, Melvyn Bragg and his guests discuss dark matter, the mysterious and invisible substance existing throughout the Universe. In 1932 the Dutch astronomer Jan Oort noticed that the speed at which galaxies moved was at odds with the amount of material they appeared to contain. He hypothesized that much of this 'missing' matter was simply invisible to telescopes. Today astronomers and particle physicists are still fascinated by the search for dark matter and the question of what it is. One leading theory is that Dark Matter is made up of WIMPS (Weakly Interacting Massive Particles) that are big, heavy and move slowly, interacting with gravity but not other particles. Scientists have developed multiple theories about the make up of this substance, and they are able to test them through remarkable computer modelling that simulates the construction of the universe. shone in the Mexican-American War, only   
to face poverty and obscurity afterward.   
He was 42 when Lee surrendered to him,   
securing victory for the Union. In 1868,

Grant’s dramatic sequences run longer

from interviews with Grant biographer Ron   
Chernow, retired U.S. Army general David   
Petraeus and other well-chosen experts.

Despite it being December with Christmas just around the corner, several decades saw some major new programming this week across networks, cable and streaming. 1965 saw the debut of two game shows that would have long runs and become classics, with one having a momentary bit of very dark history. 1975 saw the network debut of a Norman Lear sitcom that also had a long run, and was rebooted fifty years later. 2005 produced a controversial cable animated program, and a big money primetime game show that ran for multiple seasons across a major network, Syndication and Cable TV. Among the 2015 premieres were a highly regarded science fiction series that had a home on cable and streaming, and an animated series based on its creators stand-up comedy. Scroll down to see all of the shows that premiered this week and tell us if any of your favorites are celebrating milestone anniversaries.

#### 1955
*   _No new series premiered this week in 1955._

#### 1965
Barris Industries
*   December 20 – _The Dating Game_ (ABC, Eight seasons, last broadcast on July 6, 1973)  
*   December 20 – _Supermarket Sweep_ (ABC, Two seasons, last broadcast on July 14, 1967)

#### 1965
Though _The Dating Game_ ended on ABC in July 1973, the show carried on in Syndication for one more year as _The New Dating Game_. It has since been revived four times to date, from 1978-1980, 1986-1989 and 1996-1999, all in Syndication, with a single season, _The Celebrity Dating Game_, in 2021 on ABC. Jim Lange hosted the entire original ABC run, as well as the 1973 and 1978 Syndicated editions. Elaine Joyce hosted the 1986 revival in its first season, with Jeff MacGregor taking over for the remaining two seasons. Brad Sherwood hosted the first season of the 1996 revival with a format change, with Chuck Woolery hosting the final two seasons which reverted back to the original format. The show was often paired with _The Newlywed Game_ in Syndication, and the 1996 revivals of both shows were sold to stations as _The Dating/Newlywed Hour_. The original series was broadcast in black-and-white until a primetime version launched in color in 1966, making the daytime version the first ABC daytime series to be broadcast regularly in color. The show featured contestants before they became famous, including Farrah Fawcett, Suzanne Somers, Yvonne Craig, Lindsay Wagner, Leif Garrett, Tom Selleck, Lee Majors, the Carpenters, Jackson Bostwick, Michael Richards, Joanna Cameron, Andy Kaufman in his Foreign Man persona (under the pseudonym Baji Kimran), Steve Martin, Burt Reynolds, John Ritter, Phil Hartman, Jennifer Granholm (governor of Michigan from 2003 to 2010), and Arnold Schwarzenegger. Some contestants appeared on the show after they had gained fame including Michael Jackson, Burton Cummings, Dusty Springfield, Ron Howard, Maureen McCormick, Barry Williams, Sally Field, Richard Dawson, Jay North, Ted Bessell, Angela Cartwright, and Paul Lynde. Rodney Alcala appeared on the show at the same time he was on a killing spree in Los Angeles. He was selected by the bachelorette, but she ultimately refused to go out with him because she found him ‘creepy’.

#### 1965
Fellow bachelor Jed Mills described him as ‘a very strange guy’ with ‘bizarre opinions’. Unlike game shows of the era, it is assumed the entire ABC run exists in its entirety. Various episodes from the ABC daytime version have aired on Game Show Network.
_Supermarket Sweep_ was revived on the Lifetime network from February 5, 1990 to June 16, 1995, the PAX network from April 5, 1999 to May 23, 2003, and on ABC from October 18, 2020 to January 30, 2022. The 1960s _Supermarket Sweep_ was broadcast from Food Fair supermarkets, mostly around New York City. For the Lifetime version, a mock supermarket was created at Hollywood Center Studios. The show’s most famous host, Dave Ruprecht, was the Lifetime/PAX version host.

#### 1975
T.A.T. Communications Company
*   December 16 – _One Day at a Time_ (CBS, Nine seasons, 209 episodes)

#### 1975
_One Day at a Time_ was created by husband-and-wife writing duo Allan Manings and Whitney Blake. Both had been actors, with Blake most famous for her role as Dorothy Baxter on the 1960s sitcom _Hazel_. The show was based on Blake’s own life as a single mother raising her three children (including daughter Meredith Baxter) after her divorce. Two pilots were produced, with the first one shot under the title _Three to Get Ready_. The mother, Ann Romano, only had one daughter and worked as a nurse in that version. The concept was reworked and the second pilot sold. Polly Cutter sang the theme song, ‘This Is It’. Bonnie Franklin, Pat Harrington Jr., and Valerie Bertinelli were the only cast members to remain with the series throughout its entire run. Mackenzie Phillips was fired after the fifth season due to growing problems with substance abuse. She later returned in a frequent recurring role, but was let go again shortly after the start of the final season. Richard Masur was written out early in Season 2, but returned in a guest role in the Season 6 finale. Masur had played a love interest for Franklin’s character. Mary Louise Wilson replaced Masur as neighbor Ginny Wroblicki, a comedic foil for Ann, but ratings declined with her arrival and the character was unpopular with viewers. Wilson herself did not like the character, or the dramatic moral dilemma the character was given — each character had to have some moral dilemma — and she did not get along with Franklin. After 14 episodes, Normal Lear released her from her contract at her own request, and the character was never spoken of again save for a Season 5 retrospective episode. Recurring characters filled the vacancy for the next two seasons, including Joseph Campanella as Ann’s ex-husband and the girls’ father. Michael Lembeck joined in Season 5 as Julie’s husband, but was written out after Phillips was fired. He did return in Season 7 with Phillips. Ron Rifkin and Glenn Scarpelli joined the series, with Rifkin’s Nick becoming Ann’s boyfriend before the character was killed off in a car accident. Scarpelli, as Nick’s son Alex, remained with the family for the next two seasons. Shelley Fabares went from guest star to regular, and Nanette Fabray, as Ann’s mother, made more appearances before becoming a regular in Season 9.

#### 1975
Howard Hesseman joined the series for a short time and became Ann’s second husband. Phillips was fired again in the final season due to her erratic behavior, her character still referred to but not seen, with Lembeck remaining on the show as her husband. Pat Harrington won a Golden Globe in 1980 and an Emmy in 1984 for Outstanding Supporting Actor as building super Schneider. Valerie Bertinelli won Supporting Actress Emmys in 1981 and 1982. Alan Rafkin won an Emmy for Outstanding Directing in a Comedy Series in 1982. The main cast, including Phillips, reunited for a retrospective special in 2005, with various cast members also sharing their thoughts about the show in interviews. Franklin, Phillips, Bertinelli, and Harrington reunited once again on the _Today_ show in February 2008. ## Review: THE OFFICE: COMPLETE SERIES(Blu-ray)
April 24, 2023
TV Comedy, TV-14
**Grade: A-**
**TV comedy**
**Not rated**
Maybe it’s because the series is in perpetual rerun. Maybe it’s the popularity of Steve Carell ever since he turned up on moviegoers’ radar with _The 40-Year-Old Virgin._ Or maybe, like all classic comedies, it’s because the ensemble cast is fantastic from top to bottom. Whatever the case, younger viewers have discovered the American version of the popular British TV show, and Parrot Analytics reported that the audience demand for **_The Office_** (US version) is a whopping 36.3 times more in demand than the average TV series in the US.
_The Office_ also might be the most successful American TV adaptation of a British television comedy _ever_—and that’s saying something, since _Veep, Shameless, Sanford and Son, Three’s Company,_ and _All in the Family_ were all based on Britcoms. It’s certainly the longest running, with 188 episodes first airing from 2005-2013.
Two years before this documentary-style sitcom was removed from the Netflix lineup in 2021, _The Office_ was the most watched show on the streaming service. Even recently a _Cosmopolitan_ writer intoned, “How dare you, Netflix?” Fans hold grudges, especially when they no longer know where they can see the show. _Cosmo_ reported that the first five seasons of _The Office_ are now free on Peacock, but you’ll need Peacock Premium/Plus (a paid level) to watch the rest of the show.
Or, if you don’t want to keep jumping from streaming service to streaming service like an _Office_ groupie, you could just plunk down the cash to get the entire series on high-definition Blu-ray. It looks terrific and comes with a bundle of fun bonus features.

## Review: THE OFFICE: COMPLETE SERIES(Blu-ray)
Everyone who punches in at the Scranton branch office of Dunder Mifflin Paper Company is a bona fide _character._ In 2007 and 2008 the show won for Outstanding Performance by an Ensemble in a Comedy Series from peers at the Screen Actors Guild, but if it were up to fans they would have had a lot more trophies to put in their case. The series began with a solid core that established the character types and dynamics that would persist throughout the series’ long run, even with cast changes:
Michael Scott (Steve Carrell) was the regional manager and a walking illustration of the Peter Principle—which theorized that members of any hierarchy are promoted until they reach the level at which they are no longer competent. Michael was well intentioned but clearly starved for love and adulation. He was also the reason a company needs an HR officer, because he had a habit of making outrageous and insensitive remarks.
Dwight Schrute (Rainn Wilson) was a salesman and also assistant to the regional manager, a name-only title that Michael created for his favorite disciple, who happened to be Amish and also ran a beet farm with his reclusive and equally odd brother.
Pam Beesly (Jenna Fischer) was the girl-next-door type who worked as a receptionist and, though shy and reserved, could be persuaded to help with office pranks. For six years or so her and Jim’s mutual office attraction added a romantic tension.
Jim Halpert (John Krasinski) was a salesman who was both a quintessential nice guy and an inveterate practical joker, with Dwight his favorite target and Pam the object of his affection.
Stanley Hudson (Leslie David Baker) was a salesman who made his quota and nothing more, with a dry sense of humor directed at anyone who disrupted his blissful routine. He also easily tired of Michael’s constant references to him being African American.
Phyllis Lapin (Phyllis Smith) appeared older and more reserved than she actually was, and her full figure was often the target of Michael’s unintentional insults—misplaced assurances that she’s actually attractive.
Meredith Palmer (Kate Flannery) was the wild one in the office, an openly flirtatious and promiscuous supply relations representative who could throw innuendos like others throw shade.

## Review: THE OFFICE: COMPLETE SERIES(Blu-ray)
Angela Martin (Angela Kinsey) was just the opposite of Meredith, an ultra-religious conservative and cat-lover who sometimes smuggled one of her cats into her desk.
Kevin Malone (Brian Baumgartner) was the sweetheart of the group, a large, not-terribly-bright man whose humor, as with Michael’s, tended toward the juvenile.
Oscar Martinez (Oscar Nunez) was a gay Latinx man trying to keep a low profile, for the most part, though often Michael wouldn’t let him.
Creed Bratton (Creed Bratton) was the quality assurance guy who was a little on the shady side—or at least his eyebrow-raising suggestions suggested as much.
Other characters introduced later who logged a lot of episodes included Kelly Kapoor (Mindy Kaling), Ryan Howard (B.J. Novak), Andy Bernard (Ed Helms), Toby Flenderson (Paul Lieberstein), Darryl Philbin (Craig Robinson), and Erin Hannon (Ellie Kemper). Robert California (James Spader), Nellie Bertram (Catherine Tate), Jo Bennett (Kathy Bates), and Holly Flax (Amy Ryan) also had recurring roles, and Deangelo Vickers (Will Ferrell) appeared briefly.
A day at _The Office_ could turn into just about anything: challenges, drills, Olympics, debates, mandatory meetings, sensitivity training, demonstrations that had little to do with selling paper, “bonding” experiences, outings, romances—everything except for actual work, it seemed.
Each season in this set comes in its own Blu-ray case, and the nine cases are housed in a colorful slipcase. The 188 episode titles and two-line descriptions are printed on the insides of the covers, visible through the blue plastic cases—not the most convenient, but better than nothing.
Bonus features include in-character productions such as Dwight’s music video, Michael Scott’s Dunder Mifflin ad, Dunder Mifflin PSAs like “Rabies: The More You Know,” plus extended episodes, blooper reels, _Office_ webisodes, original cast audition tapes, table reads, cast farewells, and commentary tracks. Title: 10 Best Sci-Fi Shows With More Than 100 Episodes
Chunks: 0,1,2,3,4
BBC Studios
Sci-fi may very well be one the hardest genres on television to keep alive. Its shows can be pricey to make, challenging to market, and quick to get canceled, so the ones that reach 100 episodes deserve some recognition.
That kind of staying power is incredibly rare in this era of television, which is why it became the basis for this list, where every sci-fi show reached over 100 episodes. The longevity rule disqualified some of the genre's most treasured titles. "Firefly" gained a cult following and even led to a film, but was canceled way too soon, with only 14 episodes produced."Battlestar Galactica," for its part, spawned a prequel and a pair of companion films, but wrapped with fewer than 80 episodes. Even "Fringe," it turns out, bowed out with its 100th episode.
But none of the shows that ultimately made the cut simply coasted. Several outlasted cast turnover, network changes, even a cancellation. Among them: a 1959 anthology that influenced countless shows in the years that followed, a sequel series set aboard a starship that expanded a franchise, and a procedural that turned out to be about A.I. Here are 10 shows that earned every minute of their airtime.

## The Twilight Zone
Bettmann/Getty
Before "The Twilight Zone," Rod Serling spent the late '50s seeing his scripts get reworked beyond recognition by executives wary of alienating customers, including his 1956 teleplay inspired by the murder of Emmett Till that aired without its original Southern setting. His genius solution: Stop writing about the present and start writing about the unknown.
"The Twilight Zone" premiered in 1959 with Serling as its host, narrator, and the writer of many of its 156 episodes. Each one features a new story brought to life by a new cast, from a nervous flier who spots a gremlin on the plane's wing to a bookworm who gets all the time in the world to read. Many up-and-comingmovie stars appeared on "The Twilight Zone,"including Robert Redford, Robert Duvall, and Burt Reynolds.
What makes the show so powerful, and even haunting, is just how much it accomplishes in any one episode. Its twists made the series famous, but they arguably land because the episodes offer believable characters trapped in scenarios that resonate, whether it's a man desperate for solitude or neighbors on a street who come to distrust one another. The show also snuck in social commentary that sponsors overlooked, dressing up real-world fears as alien invaders, for example, and largely getting away with it. Sharp viewers, however, knew better. "The Twilight Zone" ultimately won three Emmys, including two for outstanding writing achievement in drama, and many shows, including "Black Mirror," have aired in its shadow.

## Doctor Who
BBC Studios
One of sci-fi's most acclaimed shows became known for a twist born from necessity. When the health of "Doctor Who" star William Hartnell failed, the producers decided their alien hero could cheat death, inhabiting a new body. Patrick Troughton took over in 1966, and "Doctor Who" has pulled the same trick many times over, allowing a range of actors to play the character, from Tom Baker and Sylvester McCoy to David Tennant and Jodie Whittaker.
The show's format, thankfully, is as creative as its casting. The TARDIS, a time machine disguised as a '60s London police box, can land anywhere. This means that while one week brings a historical drama, the next features a war with the Daleks, the pepper-pot killers who've hounded the Doctor since the show's second serial. The series was shelved in 1989 after 26 seasons, and apart from a 1996 TV movie, that seemed to be that. Then, showrunner Russell T Davies revived "Doctor Who" in 2005, this time with Christopher Eccleston as the lead.
With more than 800 episodes across both eras, the show holds the Guinness World Records title for most prolific science-fiction TV series. It is currently on hiatus, however. Ncuti Gatwa's Doctor regenerated into a version played by Billie Piper in May 2025, a twist yet to be explained. This June, a Christmas special was canceled and Davies exited the series. Still, if "Doctor Who" has proven anything, it's that the Doctor is nothing if not persistent.

## Star Trek: The Next Generation
CBS Television
Creator Gene Roddenberry could have simply reunited the cast of "The Original Series" for "Star Trek: The Next Generation." Instead, his ambitious follow-up jumped nearly a century ahead to a new U.S.S. Enterprise. And this starship's captain, Jean-Luc Picard (Patrick Stewart), is a far cry from James T. Kirk. If Kirk is cavalier, Picard prefers diplomatic discussions.
Decades later, the reputation of "The Next Generation" rests on episodes like "The Best of Both Worlds," the two-parter in which the Borg assimilate Picard and turn him against the Federation. It was the franchise's first real season-ending cliffhanger. The show also manages indelible storytelling moments in episodes largely set outside the Enterprise, whether it is a glimpse at Picard's slow, painful recovery from his Borg experience in "Family," or when Picard experiences decades of the life of a deceased scientist in "The Inner Light."
"The Next Generation" ultimately ran seven seasons, four more than "The Original Series," and won 17 Emmys, all in craft categories like outstanding individual achievement in special visual effects.But just as important, it proved Star Trek could still explore strange new worlds and civilizations without Kirk and Spock — and prosper. In doing so, it opened a door, with later years bringing spin-offs and films, from "Deep Space Nine" and "Voyager," to "Discovery," "Lower Decks," and "Strange New Worlds."

## The X-Files
20th Century Fox
With "The X-Files," creator Chris Carter turned an unglamorous basement office at FBI headquarters into one of the most iconic settings in '90s television. Agent Fox Mulder (David Duchovny), a true believer in extraterrestrials, was paired with Dana Scully (Gillian Anderson), a medical doctor. No two cases are alike, and many defy the laws of nature. One episode features a mutant who can squeeze through vents, while another follows an insurance salesman who foresees others' deaths.
While the cases are remarkable, Carter's real ingenuity lies in the show's structure. "The X-Files" deftly moves between "monster of the week" episodes and installments that advance the show's longer-running alien conspiracy, and in doing so, offers a structural blueprint that arguably influenced later shows like "Fringe" and "Supernatural." The series is also unafraid to experiment, with episodes like Season 5's "The Post-Modern Prometheus" shot in black and white, or Season 7's "X-Cops," which was filmed like a tongue-in-cheek reality show.
"The X-Files" finished its original run in 2002, but that wasn't the last time viewers heard from Mulder and Scully. Duchovny and Anderson reprised their roles for Season 10 in 2016 and Season 11 in 2018, bringing the show's total number of episodes to 218. The awards recognition came too, with five Golden Globes including best television series – drama. The show ultimately spawned two films and the spin-off "The Lone Gunmen," with Hulu ordering a reboot series from Ryan Coogler to star Danielle Deadwyler and Himesh Patel.

Though _The Dating Game_ ended on ABC in July 1973, the show carried on in Syndication for one more year as _The New Dating Game_. #### 1975
_One Day at a Time_ was created by husband-and-wife writing duo Allan Manings and Whitney Blake. Both had been actors, with Blake most famous for her role as Dorothy Baxter on the 1960s sitcom _Hazel_. The show was based on Blake’s own life as a single mother raising her three children (including daughter Meredith Baxter) after her divorce. Two pilots were produced, with the first one shot under the title _Three to Get Ready_. The mother, Ann Romano, only had one daughter and worked as a nurse in that version. The concept was reworked and the second pilot sold. Polly Cutter sang the theme song, ‘This Is It’. Bonnie Franklin, Pat Harrington Jr., and Valerie Bertinelli were the only cast members to remain with the series throughout its entire run. Mackenzie Phillips was fired after the fifth season due to growing problems with substance abuse. She later returned in a frequent recurring role, but was let go again shortly after the start of the final season. Richard Masur was written out early in Season 2, but returned in a guest role in the Season 6 finale. Masur had played a love interest for Franklin’s character. Mary Louise Wilson replaced Masur as neighbor Ginny Wroblicki, a comedic foil for Ann, but ratings declined with her arrival and the character was unpopular with viewers. Wilson herself did not like the character, or the dramatic moral dilemma the character was given — each character had to have some moral dilemma — and she did not get along with Franklin. After 14 episodes, Normal Lear released her from her contract at her own request, and the character was never spoken of again save for a Season 5 retrospective episode. Recurring characters filled the vacancy for the next two seasons, including Joseph Campanella as Ann’s ex-husband and the girls’ father. Michael Lembeck joined in Season 5 as Julie’s husband, but was written out after Phillips was fired. He did return in Season 7 with Phillips. Ron Rifkin and Glenn Scarpelli joined the series, with Rifkin’s Nick becoming Ann’s boyfriend before the character was killed off in a car accident. Scarpelli, as Nick’s son Alex, remained with the family for the next two seasons. Shelley Fabares went from guest star to regular, and Nanette Fabray, as Ann’s mother, made more appearances before becoming a regular in Season 9.

"The X-Files" deftly moves between "monster of the week" episodes and installments that advance the show's longer-running alien conspiracy, and in doing so, offers a structural blueprint that arguably influenced later shows like "Fringe" and "Supernatural." The series is also unafraid to experiment, with episodes like Season 5's "The Post-Modern Prometheus" shot in black and white, or Season 7's "X-Cops," which was filmed like a tongue-in-cheek reality show.
"The X-Files" finished its original run in 2002, but that wasn't the last time viewers heard from Mulder and Scully. Duchovny and Anderson reprised their roles for Season 10 in 2016 and Season 11 in 2018, bringing the show's total number of episodes to 218. The awards recognition came too, with five Golden Globes including best television series – drama. The show ultimately spawned two films and the spin-off "The Lone Gunmen," with Hulu ordering a reboot series from Ryan Coogler to star Danielle Deadwyler and Himesh Patel.

Maybe it’s because the series is in perpetual rerun. Maybe it’s the popularity of Steve Carell ever since he turned up on moviegoers’ radar with _The 40-Year-Old Virgin._ Or maybe, like all classic comedies, it’s because the ensemble cast is fantastic from top to bottom. Whatever the case, younger viewers have discovered the American version of the popular British TV show, and Parrot Analytics reported that the audience demand for **_The Office_** (US version) is a whopping 36.3 times more in demand than the average TV series in the US.
_The Office_ also might be the most successful American TV adaptation of a British television comedy _ever_—and that’s saying something, since _Veep, Shameless, Sanford and Son, Three’s Company,_ and _All in the Family_ were all based on Britcoms. It’s certainly the longest running, with 188 episodes first airing from 2005-2013.
Two years before this documentary-style sitcom was removed from the Netflix lineup in 2021, _The Office_ was the most watched show on the streaming service. Even recently a _Cosmopolitan_ writer intoned, “How dare you, Netflix?” Fans hold grudges, especially when they no longer know where they can see the show. _Cosmo_ reported that the first five seasons of _The Office_ are now free on Peacock, but you’ll need Peacock Premium/Plus (a paid level) to watch the rest of the show.
Or, if you don’t want to keep jumping from streaming service to streaming service like an _Office_ groupie, you could just plunk down the cash to get the entire series on high-definition Blu-ray. It looks terrific and comes with a bundle of fun bonus features.

## Review: THE OFFICE: COMPLETE SERIES(Blu-ray)
Everyone who punches in at the Scranton branch office of Dunder Mifflin Paper Company is a bona fide _character._ In 2007 and 2008 the show won for Outstanding Performance by an Ensemble in a Comedy Series from peers at the Screen Actors Guild, but if it were up to fans they would have had a lot more trophies to put in their case. The series began with a solid core that established the character types and dynamics that would persist throughout the series’ long run, even with cast changes:
Michael Scott (Steve Carrell) was the regional manager and a walking illustration of the Peter Principle—which theorized that members of any hierarchy are promoted until they reach the level at which they are no longer competent. Michael was well intentioned but clearly starved for love and adulation. He was also the reason a company needs an HR officer, because he had a habit of making outrageous and insensitive remarks.
Dwight Schrute (Rainn Wilson) was a salesman and also assistant to the regional manager, a name-only title that Michael created for his favorite disciple, who happened to be Amish and also ran a beet farm with his reclusive and equally odd brother.
Pam Beesly (Jenna Fischer) was the girl-next-door type who worked as a receptionist and, though shy and reserved, could be persuaded to help with office pranks. For six years or so her and Jim’s mutual office attraction added a romantic tension.
Jim Halpert (John Krasinski) was a salesman who was both a quintessential nice guy and an inveterate practical joker, with Dwight his favorite target and Pam the object of his affection.
Stanley Hudson (Leslie David Baker) was a salesman who made his quota and nothing more, with a dry sense of humor directed at anyone who disrupted his blissful routine. He also easily tired of Michael’s constant references to him being African American.
Phyllis Lapin (Phyllis Smith) appeared older and more reserved than she actually was, and her full figure was often the target of Michael’s unintentional insults—misplaced assurances that she’s actually attractive.
Meredith Palmer (Kate Flannery) was the wild one in the office, an openly flirtatious and promiscuous supply relations representative who could throw innuendos like others throw shade.

## Review: THE OFFICE: COMPLETE SERIES(Blu-ray)
Angela Martin (Angela Kinsey) was just the opposite of Meredith, an ultra-religious conservative and cat-lover who sometimes smuggled one of her cats into her desk.
Kevin Malone (Brian Baumgartner) was the sweetheart of the group, a large, not-terribly-bright man whose humor, as with Michael’s, tended toward the juvenile.
Oscar Martinez (Oscar Nunez) was a gay Latinx man trying to keep a low profile, for the most part, though often Michael wouldn’t let him.
Creed Bratton (Creed Bratton) was the quality assurance guy who was a little on the shady side—or at least his eyebrow-raising suggestions suggested as much.
Other characters introduced later who logged a lot of episodes included Kelly Kapoor (Mindy Kaling), Ryan Howard (B.J. Novak), Andy Bernard (Ed Helms), Toby Flenderson (Paul Lieberstein), Darryl Philbin (Craig Robinson), and Erin Hannon (Ellie Kemper). Robert California (James Spader), Nellie Bertram (Catherine Tate), Jo Bennett (Kathy Bates), and Holly Flax (Amy Ryan) also had recurring roles, and Deangelo Vickers (Will Ferrell) appeared briefly.
A day at _The Office_ could turn into just about anything: challenges, drills, Olympics, debates, mandatory meetings, sensitivity training, demonstrations that had little to do with selling paper, “bonding” experiences, outings, romances—everything except for actual work, it seemed.
Each season in this set comes in its own Blu-ray case, and the nine cases are housed in a colorful slipcase. The 188 episode titles and two-line descriptions are printed on the insides of the covers, visible through the blue plastic cases—not the most convenient, but better than nothing.
Bonus features include in-character productions such as Dwight’s music video, Michael Scott’s Dunder Mifflin ad, Dunder Mifflin PSAs like “Rabies: The More You Know,” plus extended episodes, blooper reels, _Office_ webisodes, original cast audition tapes, table reads, cast farewells, and commentary tracks. There’s a _lot_ here for fans to enjoy.
**Entire family: No (younger kids won’t respond to the largely adult humor)**
